rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Omission of Rule 96(10): Finality to an unnecessary GST export refund litigation
rows.desc: Supreme Court Holds Omitted Rule 96(10) Applies to Pending GST Refund Proceedings Summary: The controversy concerns the effect of omission of Rule 96(10) of the CGST Rules, 2017 on pending disputes relating to IGST refunds on exports. Rule 96(10) restricted refund of IGST paid on exports where specified exemption or concessional benefits had been availed. The Government omitted Rule 96(10), along with Rules 89(4A) and 89(4B), through Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8-10-2024. The Gujarat High Court in Addwrap Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India, the Delhi High Court in Vinayak International Housewares (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India, and the Bombay High Court in Hikal Limited v. Union of India considered the impact of the omission on pending proceedings. The controversy was ultimately resolved by the Supreme Court in Goodluck India Limited & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors., 2026 INSC 821, decided on 6-8-2026, holding that omission of Rule 96(10), in the absence of a saving clause, applies to pending proceedings. The Supreme Court rejected the contention that the GST Council’s recommendation for prospective omission preserved pending proceedings, dismissed the Revenue appeals, and dismissed the connected SLPs challenging the vires of Rule 96(10) as infructuous. Consequently, proceedings under Rule 96(10) which had not attained finality on 8-10-2024 cannot continue merely on the basis of the omitted restriction. Table of Contents▸ Introduction What Rule 96(10) sought to achieve? Government itself ultimately reconsidered restriction Prospective omission does not necessarily mean survival of pending proceedings 5. Constitution Bench principle in Kolhapur Canesugar Works Importance of absence of a saving clause Gujarat High Court: Addwrap Packaging and connected cases Delhi High Court extends the principle to SCNs, orders and appeals Line of High Court decisions is becoming increasingly consistent GST Council recommendation cannot substitute statutory text What amounts to a 'pending proceeding'? Consequences for refund claims already rejected Advance Authorisation exporters were unnecessarily caught in prolonged litigation Supreme Court finally settles controversy Why a retrospective revival would be undesirable? Omission should bring closure, not another round of litigation Conclusion Show all 17 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction The provision of Rule 96(10) of the CGST Rules, 2017 placed restrictions on refund of integrated tax paid on exports where the exporter or its supplier had availed specified exemption or concessional benefits. What was ostensibly conceived as an anti-double-benefit mechanism eventually became a significant source of litigation, particularly for exporters importing inputs under schemes such as Advance Authorisation. The controversy has now entered an important phase following the omission of Rule 96(10) by Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8-10-2024. The omission itself reflected a significant change in policy. The Government ultimately accepted that continuation of the restriction was unnecessary, and the provision disappeared from the statutory framework. The more difficult question, however, was what would happen to demands, show-cause notices, refund disputes, appeals and writ petitions relating to earlier periods which had not attained finality as on 8-10-2024. A substantial body of High Court jurisprudence has now developed in favour of exporters. The Gujarat High Court in the group of matters led by Addwrap Packaging (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India held that although the omission operates prospectively from 8-10-2024, it equally applies to proceedings which were pending on that date and had not attained finality. The Delhi High Court subsequently adopted the same approach and extended the benefit even to pending show-cause notices, orders and appeals. Similar reasoning has been adopted by other High Courts. On 6-8-2026, Supreme Court finally decided Goodluck India Limited & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors., 2026 INSC 821 and, substantially affirmed exporters’ position and settled central controversy in their favour. Court held that omission of Rule 96(10) by Notification No. 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8-10-2024 without any saving clause applies to pending proceedings. It expressly relied upon Constitution Bench judgment in Kolhapur Canesugar Works Ltd. v. Union of India, (2000) 2 SCC 536 and found no reason to interfere with High Court view. What Rule 96(10) sought to achieve? Rule 96 deals with refund of integrated tax paid on goods or services exported out of India. Under the GST framework, exports are zero-rated supplies and the legislative policy embodied in section 16 of the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 is that taxes should ordinarily not be exported. Rule 96(10), however, carved out an important restriction. Broadly stated, an exporter who had received supplies on which specified concessional or exe
rows.summary: Supreme Court held that deleting GST Rule 96(10) also ends unresolved export-refund cases, so pending proceedings can’t rely on the old restriction.

rows.title: Income Tax | Search Clock Starts on Seized Material Receipt; AYs 2011-12 & 2012-13 Outside Section 153C
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12256 Case Name DCIT Vs Rasraj Marketing Private Limited (ITAT Delhi Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2011-12 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Rasraj Marketing Private Limited (ITAT Delhi Bench) Search Clock Starts When Seized Papers Reach the “Other Person’s” AO: AYs 2011-12 & 2012-13 Fall Outside s.153C Block Background: A search u/s 132 was conducted on the Alankit Group, Shri Alok K. Agarwal, his son & certain associates on 18.10.2019. The search allegedly revealed material indicating that the group facilitated acquisition of shares in shell entities, accommodation entries & artificial short-term capital losses. Certain documents, including ledger accounts, allegedly relating to Rasraj Marketing Pvt. Ltd. were seized from the searched premises. The AO of the searched person recorded a satisfaction note on 20.12.2021. The jurisdictional AO of Rasraj Marketing recorded a separate satisfaction note on 24.12.2021, following which notices u/s 153C were issued on 28.12.2021. For AY 2011-12, the assessee had originally declared income of ₹41,310. The AO completed assessment u/s 153C on 30.03.2023, making an addition of ₹28,99,042 u/s 69A & determining total income at ₹29,40,352. A similar assessment was framed for AY 2012-13. The Crucial Question: Which Date Starts the Clock? For a person searched directly, the block under s.153A is ordinarily reckoned with reference to the previous year in which the search occurs. However, Rasraj Marketing was not searched. Proceedings were initiated because documents seized from another person were claimed to relate to it. Therefore, the controversy was whether the six/ten-year period should be calculated from: 18.10.2019, being the date of search on the Alankit Group; or 24/28.12.2021, when satisfaction was recorded & proceedings were initiated against Rasraj Marketing. The difference was decisive. If the search date governed, the disputed years could potentially fall within the extended block. If the date on which the other person’s AO received the material governed, the relevant base year became AY 2022-23, making AYs 2011-12 & 2012-13 too old. CIT(A) Follows Ojjus Medicare The CIT(A) relied upon the jurisdictional Delhi High Court’s judgment in PCIT v. Ojjus Medicare Pvt. Ltd., 465 ITR 101. The High Court held that for proceedings against an “other person” u/s 153C, the date of search must be deemed to be the date on which the seized books, documents or assets are received by the AO having jurisdiction over that other person. Applying that principle, the CIT(A) treated December 2021 as the relevant date. The associated AY was AY 2022-23. The ten-year block would accordingly cover AYs 2013-14 to 2022-23. Since AYs 2011-12 & 2012-13 preceded that block, the assessments were annulled without adjudicating the additions on merits. Revenue Relies on Finance Act, 2017 Amendment The Revenue argued that after amendments made by the Finance Act, 2017 with effect from 01.04.2017, s.153C expressly linked the six-year & extended ten-year periods to the AY relevant to the previous year in which the actual search was conducted. According to the Department, the first proviso to s.153C creates a deemed date of search based upon receipt of material only for the limited purpose of determining whether pending assessments abate. It does not shift the entire block period. The Revenue informed the Tribunal that an SLP against Ojjus Medicare was pending before the Supreme Court. However, it could not produce any order staying the operation of the Delhi High Court’s judgment. Tribunal Records Its View but Follows Binding Precedent The ITAT referred to its recent decision in DCIT v. Sunil Bhala, which arose from the same Alankit Group search. In that decision, the Bench had undertaken a detailed examination of the post-2017 statutory provisions. Its interpretative view was that the amendment required the six/ten-year period to be reckoned from the actual search date, while the deemed receipt date under the first proviso was confined to identifying abated & unabated assessments. Nevertheless, the Tribunal recognised that it was bound by the Delhi High Court’s judgment in Ojjus Medicare. Judicial discipline required the jurisdictional High Court’s interpretation to prevail irrespective of the Tribunal’s own understanding of the amended provision. The mere filing of an SLP did not dilute the binding force of the judgment, particularly when no stay had been granted. Final Verdict Following Ojjus Medicare, the Tribunal held that the relevant block must be computed from the date on which the seized material was handed over to the AO of Rasraj Marketing. With AY 2022-23 as the reference point, the ten-year period covered AY
rows.summary: Delhi ITAT held search-period limits for third-party tax action run from when seized material reaches that person’s tax officer, voiding older years.

rows.title: Corporate Law | SC Sets Aside Arbitrary Tender Rejection and Orders Fresh Tender Process
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12255 Case Name Banshidhar Construction Pvt. Ltd. Vs Bharat Coking Coal Limited & Others (Supreme Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Banshidhar Construction Pvt. Ltd. Vs Bharat Coking Coal Limited & Others (Supreme Court) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL) was justified in rejecting the technical bid of Banshidhar Construction Pvt. Ltd. while accepting the technical bid of Respondent No. 8, despite the latter having failed to submit mandatory documents relating to the qualification criteria prescribed under Clause 10 of the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) dated 16.08.2023. BCCL had invited a tender for the project to “Re-open, salvage, rehabilitate, develop, construct and operate for excavation I extraction of coal from Amalgamated East Bhuggatdih Simlabahal Coal Mine and delivery thereof to the Authority at Bastacolla Area of BCCL” on revenue-sharing basis for twenty-five years. The Appellant submitted its bid on 29.11.2023. Its technical bid was rejected on 06.05.2024 on the stated ground that it did not comply with Clause 10 of the NIT concerning the Power of Attorney for signing the bid. The technical bids had been opened on 04.12.2023, while the last date for submission was 01.12.2023. The Appellant contended that its Director, Lalti Devi, had been authorised by Board Resolution dated 07.11.2023 and a Power of Attorney was executed in her favour on the same date. Although the Power of Attorney was notarised on 14.11.2023, it and the other requisite documents were uploaded before the last date of submission. It was argued that rejection of the Appellant’s bid was arbitrary, particularly because Respondent No. 8 had itself failed to submit scanned copies of the audited balance sheets required under Clause 10 in relation to financial capacity. Those documents were subsequently submitted on 17.04.2024 after the technical bids had already been opened. BCCL argued that the Appellant’s mandatory bid documents had been signed on 13.11.2023 whereas the Power of Attorney was notarised only on 14.11.2023, and therefore the signatory lacked the requisite authority when the documents were signed. It further contended that Respondent No. 8 had merely furnished shortfall documents pursuant to a clarification sought during evaluation and had not been permitted to replace its bid documents. The Supreme Court examined Clause 10 of the NIT and found that the scanned copies of the audited annual reports for the last three financial years were mandatory qualification documents. Respondent No. 8 admittedly had not submitted those documents with its bid before the stipulated deadline and furnished them only after a clarification was sought. The Court therefore found no justification for accepting Respondent No. 8’s technical bid while rejecting the Appellant’s bid for alleged non-compliance with the same mandatory clause. As regards the Appellant’s Power of Attorney, the Court held that the relevant requirement was that the Power of Attorney be submitted in the prescribed format and duly notarised/certified as required by the NIT. The NIT nowhere stated that the Power of Attorney had to be notarised before the bid documents were signed. Since the Power of Attorney had been executed on 07.11.2023, was subsequently notarised on 14.11.2023 and was submitted along with the requisite documents before the last date, the Court found no legal or justifiable basis for rejecting the Appellant’s technical bid. The Court also referred to Section 2 of the Power Of Attorney Act, 1882, concerning execution under a power of attorney. It held that the Power of Attorney executed in favour of the signatory was sufficient in the circumstances and that the Appellant had not violated the mandatory tender requirement. The Supreme Court reiterated that although judicial review in contractual and tender matters is limited and courts do not ordinarily sit as appellate authorities over tender decisions, governmental authorities and their instrumentalities must act fairly, reasonably and transparently. The Court emphasised that Article 14 of the Constitution of India prohibits arbitrary State action and requires fairness and equality in the bidding process. Applying these principles, the Court concluded that BCCL’s action in rejecting the Appellant’s technical bid on an extraneous ground while accepting Respondent No. 8’s bid despite non-compliance with the mandatory Clause 10 requirement was “totally arbitrary and illegal”. The Court also rejected the submission that the project’s infrastructure and national importance prevented judicial intervention. According to the Court, arbitrariness or discrimination in the award of a mega
rows.summary: The Supreme Court held BCCL acted arbitrarily in rejecting one bidder and allowing another to cure missing mandatory documents, and ordered a fresh tender process.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Deletes Unexplained Shop Investment Additions Based on Third-Party Evidence
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12254 Case Name Rajesh Mafatlal Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Rajesh Jain Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, disposed of cross-appeals arising from the common order dated 25.08.2023 of CIT(A)-52, Mumbai, concerning AYs 2018-19 to 2021-22. The assessee, engaged in mobile accessories business under M/s Raj Telecom, was searched under section 132 of the Act following search and seizure operations in the Rubberwala Group. Documents found with the group recorded alleged cash receipts outside the books for 21 shops in “Platinum Mall”, aggregating to Rs.5,21,01,155/- for FYs 2017-18 to 2020-21. The Assessing Officer treated the entire year-wise amounts as unexplained investment under section 69 in the assessee’s hands. The assessee contended that only Shop No.36 had been purchased in his name and that the other shops belonged to family members or other persons independently assessed to tax. The CIT(A) accepted this contention, sustaining only Rs.18,64,200/- for Shop No.36 in AY 2020-21 and deleting the remaining additions. The Revenue challenged that relief for all four years, while the assessee challenged the surviving AY 2020-21 addition. In AY 2021-22, both sides also challenged the CIT(A)’s treatment of a stock-shortage addition. For AYs 2018-19 and 2019-20, the Tribunal held that unaccounted investment is assessable in the hands of the person who actually made the investment. Since the other shops were purchased by different persons who were separately assessed to tax, and it was not shown or proved that the assessee funded their cash payments, the Tribunal agreed that any enquiry or action concerning such payments had to be against the respective purchasers. It accordingly upheld deletion of the additions on merits. The Tribunal also accepted the assessee’s alternative legal contention for the unabated years. The alleged cash-payment material was found during the search of the Rubberwala Group, not during the search of the assessee. Applying the Supreme Court’s decision in PCIT Vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd., the Tribunal held that, for unabated assessment years, additions under section 153A required incriminating material found in the search of the assessee. Material found with third parties could be acted upon through the procedure under section 153C, which had not been followed. The additions for AYs 2018-19 and 2019-20 were therefore deleted on both legal grounds and merits. For AY 2020-21, the Revenue’s challenge to the CIT(A)’s deletion of cash payments relating to shops purchased by others was rejected by applying the Tribunal’s earlier merits finding. As regards the Rs.18,64,200/- addition relating to Shop No.36, the Tribunal found that the Assessing Officer had relied on documents and a statement originating from the third party search, without corroborative material, while the assessee had denied making the payment. The Assessing Officer had also failed to provide the requested cross-examination of the Rubberwala Group persons. Relying on the principle stated in Naren Premchang Nagda and the Supreme Court’s decision in Andaman Timber Industries, the Tribunal held that the addition could not be sustained and directed its deletion. The assessee’s challenge to the assessment under section 153A/need for section 153C was rejected for AY 2020-21 because that year was an abated assessment and the Assessing Officer could consider other material during assessment; consequently, non-initiation of section 153C did not prevent consideration of material obtained from the Rubberwala Group search. For AY 2021-22, the Tribunal again upheld the CIT(A)’s relief concerning shops purchased by others. On stock shortage, physical stock found during search was valued at Rs.33,83,233/- against book stock of Rs.1,05,06,534/-, resulting in a shortage of Rs.71,23,301/-. The assessee attributed the shortage to destruction of stock in a fire at City Centre in October 2020 and furnished a quantity-based reconciliation. The Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and treated the entire shortage as unaccounted sales. The CIT(A) accepted that only the profit element could be taxed and applied a 4.48% gross profit rate, sustaining Rs.3,19,124/-. The Tribunal observed that the assessee had not supported the fire-loss reconciliation with evidence, but equally found that the Revenue’s conclusion that the shortage represented unaccounted sales was based only on presumption. It further noted that the assessment order did not explain how book stock had been valued despite the assessee’s books apparently not reflecting the fire loss. The Tribunal therefore set aside the CIT(A)’s order on this
rows.summary: ITAT Mumbai deleted most unexplained-investment additions, ruling third-party search material needed direct proof, and upheld only limited relief-adjusted stock shortage tax.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Jharkhand HC Sets Aside GST Order Passed Against Dead Proprietor
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12253 Case Name S.B. Enterprises Vs Directorate General of GST Intelligence (Jharkhand High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Jharkhand High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); S.B. Enterprises Vs Directorate General of GST Intelligence (Jharkhand High Court) Summary: The Jharkhand High Court considered a challenge to an order-in-original dated 23rd January, 2026 passed against Late Shibu Prasad Das, the sole proprietor of M/s S.B. Enterprises, despite his death on 15th September, 2020. The writ petition was filed through his son, Monty Kumar, who represented the proprietary concern. The petitioner submitted that the respondents were aware of the proprietor’s death but nevertheless passed the order against him. It was contended that an order made against a dead person was a nullity and could not be enforced against his representative. Reliance was also placed on an earlier order dated 24th January, 2025 in W.P.(T) No.265 of 2025, where a coordinate Bench of the Court had stayed further proceedings pursuant to a similar order-in-original made after the death of Shibu Prasad Das. The petitioner pointed out that the same respondents had been heard in that earlier proceeding. The respondents contended that the order had been made against a proprietary firm which continued to survive. They also submitted that there was nothing on record showing that the department had been specifically informed about the proprietor’s death. The High Court found the impugned order-in-original dated 23rd January, 2026 vulnerable because it had been made against a dead person. The Court expressly declined, at that stage, to enter into the disputed question of whether specific intimation of the death had been given to the department. However, it considered the earlier order dated 24th January, 2025 significant because it had been passed after hearing the very same respondents. The Court observed that the respondents could not claim ignorance of the earlier order, particularly when that order had stayed further proceedings concerning an order made against the same deceased person. Despite this, the Department had, almost a year later, made another order against him. The Court rejected the relevance of the contention that the proprietary firm continued to exist. At least prima facie, the case concerned a proprietary concern, and once the proprietor had expired, the department was required to give notice to the legal representative if it wished to proceed further. The Court found that this had not been done. Accordingly, the High Court quashed and set aside the order-in-original dated 23rd January, 2026. At the same time, it left it open to the respondents to take such steps as they might be advised, in accordance with law, to pursue their claims against the petitioner. The writ petition was disposed of on these terms, the rule was made absolute, and no order as to costs was passed. Cases Discussed W.P.(T) No.265 of 2025, order dated 24th January, 2025, Jharkhand High Court. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF JHARKHAND HIGH COURT 1. Heard learned counsel for the parties. 2. We issue Rule in this petition. With the consent and at the request of learned counsel for the parties, the rule is made returnable forthwith. 3. The petitioner is a proprietary concern, now represented by Mr. Monty Kumar, son of Late Shibu Prasad Das, Deoghar, Jharkhand. 4. The petitioner states that the sole proprietor of the petitioner-firm was late Shibu Prasad Das, who expired on 15th September, 2020. 5. Mrs Darshana Poddar Mishra, learned counsel for the petitioner, submits that though the respondents were aware that Shibu Prasad Das had expired on 15th September, 2020, an order-in-original dated 23rd January, 2026 was made against him. She further submits that such an order is a nullity and cannot be enforced against the representative of the petitioner (Mr Monty Kumar), who is the son of Late Shibu Prasad Das. 6. Mrs Darshana Poddar Mishra placed on record the order dated 24th January, 2025, made in W.P.(T) No.265 of 2025, in which a similar order-in-original was challenged on the ground that it was made after Shibu Prasad Das had expired. Therein, the co-ordinate Bench of this Court granted a stay of all further proceedings pursuant to the impugned orders. She submits that this order was made after hearing the learned counsel for the respondents, who are incidentally the same respondents impleaded in this petition. 7. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that an order has been made against a proprietary firm which still survives. rows.title: Excise Duty | CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund of Service Tax Paid Under Reverse Charge
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12252 Case Name A Schulman Plastic India Pvt. Ltd. Vs Commissioner of C.E. & S.T. (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A Schulman Plastic India Pvt. Ltd. Vs Commissioner of C.E. & S.T. (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Ahmedabad considered the appeal filed by M/s. A Schulman Plastic India Pvt Ltd against rejection of refund claims relating to Service Tax paid under reverse charge mechanism for the period prior to 01.07.2017. During audit under Final Audit Report No. 25/2018-19, the appellant had paid Service Tax on reverse charge basis on Management, Technical Consultancy, Maintenance & Repair, Manpower Recruitment, commission, GTA and legal consultancy services amounting to Rs. 45,32,123/- for the period prior to 01.07.2017. The appellant had also paid Service Tax on reverse charge basis on ocean freight for April 2017 to June 2017 amounting to Rs. 13,97,310/-. These amounts were paid suo motu under Section 73(3) of the Finance Act, 1994, under which issuance of show cause notice and penalty was waived. As the Service Tax was paid after 01.07.2017 although it related to the period before introduction of GST, the appellant contended that the amount was eligible as CENVAT credit under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Since the credit could not be utilised under the GST regime, the appellant filed refund claims under Section 142(3) of the CGST Act, 2017. Two show cause notices dated 06.09.2018 proposed rejection of the refund claims by invoking Section 142(8)(a) of the CGST Act, 2017. The adjudicating authority rejected the refund claims through Orders-in-Original dated 29.10.2018. The Commissioner (Appeals) also rejected the appeals through Order-in-Appeal dated 07.01.2019, additionally holding that payment under Section 73(3) and Rule 9(1)(bb) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 prevented availment of credit. Before the Tribunal, the appellant submitted that the Service Tax related to the pre-GST period and was therefore eligible for CENVAT credit. Since the credit could not be utilised after 01.07.2017, Section 142(3) of the CGST Act specifically provided for cash refund. The appellant further argued that Rule 9(1)(bb) was inapplicable because no show cause notice had been issued alleging fraud, collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. It was alternatively submitted that Rule 9(1)(bb) applies to supplementary invoices, bills or challans issued by a provider of output service, whereas the present credit was based on the challan evidencing Service Tax paid by the appellant as recipient under reverse charge. The Tribunal accepted these submissions. It first held that Section 142(8) of the CGST Act concerns input tax credit under the CGST Act and does not govern refund of CENVAT credit pertaining to the pre-GST period. Since the appellant had not claimed input tax credit under the CGST Act, invocation of Section 142(8) was misplaced. Section 142(3) specifically provides for cash refund of eligible CENVAT credit relating to the existing law. The Tribunal further held that rejection of the refund with reference to Section 73(3) was beyond the scope of the show cause notice because that ground had not been proposed in the notices. The adjudicating authority therefore could not reject the refund on a ground travelling beyond the show cause notice. The Tribunal also observed that payment under Section 73(3) did not affect admissibility of CENVAT credit. The appellant had paid the Service Tax and had opted for Section 73(3), which had been accepted by the department without issuance of a show cause notice. The Tribunal noted that if suppression, wilful misstatement, collusion or fraud had been alleged, the benefit of Section 73(3) would not have been available in view of Section 73(4). No such allegation had been adjudicated upon in the present case. On Rule 9(1)(bb), the Tribunal held that the provision was not applicable. Rule 9(1)(bb) deals with a supplementary invoice, bill or challan issued by a provider of output service in specified circumstances. In the present case, Service Tax had been paid by the appellant under reverse charge and the credit was taken on the appellant’s own bank challan. Therefore, Rule 9(1)(bb) could not be invoked to deny the credit. The Tribunal relied upon the judicial decisions cited by the appellant, including the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 provisions concerning documents for CENVAT credit, and held that the judgments relied upon were directly applicable. Accordingly, the Tribunal held that the appellant was eligible for refund under Section 142(3) of the CGST Act, 2017, set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal. Cases D
rows.summary: CESTAT Ahmedabad allowed refund of pre-GST CENVAT credit for reverse-charge service tax paid by the taxpayer, rejecting the department’s denial.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs Hareshkumar Manilal Somaiya (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s appeal under section 260A of the Income Tax Act, concerning deletion of an addition of Rs. 11,69,50,000 made under section 68 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on account of unsecured loans. The assessee was proprietor of M/s. Rohit Trading Co., engaged in trading of grains and other food items. For AY 2012-13, the assessee filed his return on 29.09.2012 declaring total income of Rs. 7,05,650/-. The return was selected for scrutiny and notice under section 143(2) was issued on 22.8.2013, followed by notice under section 142(1). According to the department, the assessee did not produce the books of accounts. Consequently, assessment was completed on 17.3.2015 under section 143(3) read with section 144, determining total income at Rs. 23,01,11,530/-. Before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), the assessee challenged the assessment. The appellate Commissioner partly allowed the appeal on 28.3.2017. In relation to the addition of Rs. 11,74,50,000 under section 68, the Commissioner deleted Rs. 11,69,50,000 and confirmed Rs. 5,00,000. The Commissioner also deleted Rs. 9,55,33,843 out of the disallowance of Rs. 9,56,33,843 relating to purchases and sustained Rs. 1,00,000. The Revenue appealed to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, which dismissed the appeal. The Revenue therefore approached the High Court under section 260A. The substantial questions proposed by the Revenue concerned whether the Tribunal was justified in holding that the assessee had discharged the onus under section 68 and whether it was justified in upholding deletion of the addition of Rs. 11,69,50,000 relating to unsecured loans. The High Court noted that the appellate Commissioner had considered the Assessing Officer’s remand report dated 14.3.2017. The remand report and evidence placed on record showed that, except for unsecured loans of Rs. 50,000 and Rs. 4,50,000 received and paid in the cases of Shri Kiritkumar Somchand and Shri Mohanlal Morarji respectively, the assessee had furnished satisfactory evidence regarding the balance amounts. The appellate Commissioner accordingly deleted the balance addition. The Tribunal endorsed these findings and noted that evidence including copies of PAN, ledger accounts, confirmations, bank statements and audited books had been made available during the remand proceedings. The Tribunal found that the Assessing Officer had not pointed out any deficiency in those primary documents while holding that the assessee had failed to establish the identity of the creditors, genuineness of the transactions and creditworthiness of the creditors. The High Court held that the findings recorded by the appellate Commissioner and the Tribunal were based on material and proper appreciation thereof. They were findings of fact and were not liable to interference in the appeal. Accordingly, the Court held that the substantial questions of law proposed by the Revenue could not be said to arise. No other substantial question of law arose, and the appeal was dismissed. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF GUJARAT HIGH COURT 1. rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Rajkot Quashes Section 263 Revision for Inadequate Inquiry into Sundry Creditors
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12250 Case Name Parisharam Builders Krunal Complex Vs PCIT (ITAT Rajkot) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2015-16 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Rajkot Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Parisharam Builders Krunal Complex Vs PCIT (ITAT Rajkot) Summary: The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in civil construction mainly for government bodies, filed its return for AY 2015-16 on 31.10.2015 declaring total income of Rs. 82,64,950/-. The case was selected for Limited Scrutiny under CASS and the assessment was completed under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on 23.11.2017 accepting the returned income. The Principal Commissioner of Income-tax subsequently invoked section 263. The record showed that the Assessing Officer had called for details of outstanding sundry creditors above Rs.1 lakh, including complete addresses, PAN and details of purchases giving rise to the creditors. The PCIT considered the assessee’s response deficient because, according to him, details of purchases were not furnished and PAN, return acknowledgements and complete addresses were absent in a majority of confirmations. He also noted instances of cash payments in instalments below Rs.20,000/-. The PCIT therefore considered the assessment order erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of Revenue and directed the AO to make in-depth independent inquiries into identity, creditworthiness and genuineness. The assessee contended that complete creditor details, confirmations, ledgers and other documents had been furnished and that the AO had specifically examined the sundry creditors during assessment. It was submitted that many creditors represented opening balances, that transactions were through banking channels and that the proposed revision amounted to a change of opinion. The assessee relied, inter alia, on the principles governing revision under section 263, together with judicial precedents including Torrent Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Smt. Renuka Phillip, Parshuram Pottery Works, Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd., CIT v. Arvind Jewellers, CIT v. Max India Ltd., CIT v. Jagson International Ltd., CIT v. SakSoft Ltd. and CIT v. R.K. Construction Co. The TaxGuru discussion of revision under section 263 is available here: Revision by Commissioner – Section 263 -Income Tax Act 1961 The Tribunal distinguished between “Lack of enquiry” and “inadequate enquiry”. It observed that the PCIT himself accepted that inquiries had been conducted, while objecting that “depth independent inquires” had not been made. Relying on CIT v. Sunbeam Auto Ltd., the Tribunal held that where an inquiry has been made, even if inadequate, that by itself does not permit revision under section 263 merely because the Commissioner has a different opinion. The Tribunal also followed CIT v. Arvind Jewellers, applying the principle that where relevant material and explanations were before the AO and a particular view was taken, the mere possibility of another view cannot justify revision. The Tribunal further noted that the PCIT himself found the relevant details and evidence in the assessment record. Section 142(1) empowers the AO to call for information considered necessary for making the assessment, and the manner and extent of inquiry fall within the AO’s domain. The Tribunal therefore held that the initiation of section 263 proceedings was contrary to the settled legal position. The Tribunal also considered the actual assessment record. The AO’s notice under section 142(1) specifically sought details of all outstanding sundry creditors above Rs.1 lakh, their addresses and PAN, together with details of purchases giving rise to the creditors. The assessee responded with explanations and creditor confirmations. The Tribunal recorded that ledgers and confirmations contained details of purchases, payments and balances, that many opening balances came from earlier audited books, and that the liabilities represented purchases, services or salary payments incurred in the normal course of business. In relation to opening balances and subsequent repayments, the Tribunal noted that the opening balances represented closing balances of the preceding year which had not been doubted. It also noted that creditors included reputed companies and that some were repaid in subsequent years. In this context, it relied on CIT, Rajkot-I v. Ayachi Chandrashekhar Narsangji, where repayment accepted by the Department was treated as relevant to the genuineness of the credit. TaxGuru has an independently verified publication concerning this precedent: TaxGuru publication concerning CIT, Rajkot-I v. Ayachi Chandrashekhar Narsangji Ultimately, the Tribunal held that the AO had carried out extensive inquiries and that Explanation 2(a) to section 263(1) had no application o
rows.summary: ITAT Rajkot held that tax authorities cannot revise an assessment under section 263 just because they want deeper creditor checks when the AO already made enquiries.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Ahmedabad Deletes Section 68 Additions on Loan and Opening Creditor Balance
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12249 Case Name Dharmanandan Developers Vs ITO (ITAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dharmanandan Developers Vs ITO (ITAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The appeal by Dharmanandan Developers was directed against the order dated 06.11.2024 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, Delhi for A.Y. 2018-19. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Ahmedabad Bench, considered two additions: Rs. 25,00,000/- relating to an unsecured loan from Shri Sanjivkumar Kiritkumar Patel and Rs. 29,87,770/- relating to M/s Sai Trading Company. The appeal was ultimately allowed in full. Unsecured loan of Rs. 25,00,000/- During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had taken unsecured loans aggregating to Rs. 3,66,89,137/- from various parties. In respect of Shri Sanjivkumar Kiritkumar Patel, the Assessing Officer recorded that no response had been received to a notice issued under Section 133(6) and, therefore, treated Rs. 25,00,000/- as unexplained under Section 68. The CIT(A) accepted the identity and genuineness of the creditor but considered creditworthiness unproved. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the lender had actually responded to the notice before the assessment order and had furnished a written submission, bank statement with Vijay Co. Op. Bank Ltd. and the ledger account. The assessee also relied on the lender’s return of income showing income of Rs. 25,38,990/-. The Tribunal found that the lender had specifically responded to the notice, furnished the bank statement from which the loan was given and supplied the ledger account. It further noted the return of income declaring Rs. 25,38,990/-, which established creditworthiness. The Tribunal held that the addition had been made without reasonable basis and that the CIT(A) had not identified any specific lacuna or shortfall in the supporting evidence. Accordingly, the Rs. 25,00,000/- addition was deleted and Ground No. 1 was allowed. Sundry creditor of Rs. 29,87,770/- The second dispute concerned M/s Sai Trading Company. The Assessing Officer had issued a notice under Section 133(6), to which no response was received, and made an addition of Rs. 29,87,770/-. The CIT(A) sustained the addition, observing that the material available consisted only of the account in the assessee’s books without confirmation from the creditor. The assessee submitted that the creditor’s ledger account had already been furnished to the Assessing Officer vide letter dated 09.03.2020 and its PAN and opening and closing balances had been submitted vide letter dated 23.03.2021. It was further submitted that the amount represented an opening balance brought forward from prior assessment years. The Tribunal considered the principle stated in Ivan Singh vs. ACIT, 116 taxmann.com 499 (Bombay), where the High Court held that a credit under Section 68 is chargeable in the previous year in which the sum is credited and an outstanding credit pertaining to an earlier financial year could not be taxed in a later assessment year. The Tribunal also considered Geeri Fashions Pvt. Ltd. vs. ITO, Ward-1(2), Surat, 130 taxmann.com 495 (Surat-Tribunal), where it was held that where alleged money on account of share application or share premium was received in an earlier year, the same could not be taxed in the current financial year. Applying these judicial precedents, the Tribunal held that the sundry-creditor addition pertained to an earlier assessment year and represented only the opening balance for the year under consideration. No addition was therefore liable to be sustained. Ground No. 2 was allowed. Consequently, the Tribunal held that both disputed additions were unsustainable and allowed the assessee’s appeal in the combined result. Cases Discussed Ivan Singh vs. ACIT, Circle-1(1), 116 taxmann.com 499 (Bombay) Geeri Fashions Pvt. Ltd. vs. ITO, Ward-1(2), Surat, 130 taxmann.com 495 (Surat-Tribunal) CIT v. Bhaichand H. Gandhi, [1982] 11 Taxman 59/[1983] 141 ITR 67 CIT v. Lakshman Swaroop Gupta & Brothers, [1975] 100 ITR 222 Bhor Industries Ltd. v. CIT, [1961] 42 ITR 57 (SC) FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ITAT, AHMEDABAD This appeal has been filed by the Assessee against the order passed by the Ld. Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), (in short “Ld. CIT(A)”), National Faceless Appeal Centre (in short “NFAC”), Delhi vide order dated 06.11.2024 passed for A.Y. 2018-19. 2. The assessee has taken the following grounds of appeal: “1.1 The order passed by U/s.250 passd on 06.11.2024 by NFAC, [CIT(A)], Delhi (for short CIT(A)” upholding the addition of Rs.25,00,000/- in respect of Shri Sanjivkumar Kiritkumar Pate
rows.summary: ITAT Ahmedabad deleted Section 68 additions on a loan and an opening creditor balance, holding the taxpayer’s evidence and prior-year balance were sufficient.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chandubhai Ramjibhai Kathiriya Vs CIT (ITAT Rajkot) Summary: The appeal concerned an addition of Rs.14,32,782/- being 50% of the assessee’s agricultural income, treated by the Assessing Officer as unexplained cash credit under section 68 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 read with section 115BBE. The assessee, an individual and agriculturist, had filed his return declaring total income of Rs.340/- and agricultural income of Rs.28,65,563/- for AY 2017-18. The assessee stated that he held 19.12 acres of agricultural land and produced Form No. 7/12 and other revenue records. He also relied upon agricultural income disclosed in earlier years: Rs.14,52,800/- for AY 2015-16 and Rs.29,92,400/- for AY 2016-17, while his gross total income for those years was only Rs.663/- and Rs.123/- respectively. The Assessing Officer issued notice under section 133(6) to Radhe Fertilizer but received no response. He consequently considered 50% of the agricultural income to be reasonable and treated the balance Rs.14,32,782/- as unaccounted income introduced in the guise of exempt agricultural income. The NFAC rejected the appeal, observing that the addition was factual, the affidavit was self-serving, and supporting evidence of agricultural operations had not been produced. Before the Tribunal, the assessee relied upon his landholding, an affidavit and earlier returns showing substantial agricultural income. The Tribunal examined the statutory requirement of a credit in books for invoking section 68. It referred to Smt. Ramilaben B. Patel Vs. ITO, where the Tribunal considered that a bank statement/passbook is not books of account for section 68 purposes, and to CIT v. Bhaichand N. Gandhi (1983) 141 ITR 67 (Bom). It also followed CIT vs. Taj Borewells (2007) 291 ITR 0232, concerning the requirement of books for section 68. CIT vs Taj Borewells The Tribunal held that the lower authorities were not legally correct in invoking section 68 against the agricultural income shown by the assessee. The addition of Rs.14,32,782/- was therefore deleted and the assessee’s appeal was allowed. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT RAJKOT 1. This appeal is filed by the Assessee against the exparte Appellate order dated 26.08.2021 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, Delhi, (in short referred to as “NFAC”), as against the assessment order passed under section 143(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’) relating to the Assessment Year (A.Y) 2017-18. 2. The solitary issue before us is that the Ld. CIT(A) erred in upholding addition of Rs. 14,32,782/- being 50 percent of agricultural income treating as unexplained cash credit u/s. 68 of the Income Tax Act in the absence of books of accounts. 3. The brief facts of the case is that the assessee is an individual and agriculturist by profession filed his Return of Income on 26-07-2017 declaring the total income as Rs. 340/- and agricultural income of Rs. 28,65,563/-. The assessee case was selected for scrutiny assessment since the assessee shown large agricultural income and the assessee was requested to justify the same with necessary evidences. 3.1. The assessee replied that he was holding agricultural land measuring 19.12 acres wherein crops were grown and produced Form No. 7/12 copy and other Revenue records. The assessee also shown agricultural income for the earlier previous two Assessment Years and the Gross total income which is much less than the basic exempt income of Rs. 2,50,000/- as follows: A.Y. Gross Total Income Exemption Limit Net Agricultural Income 2017-18 340 2,50,000 28,65,563 2016-17 123 2,50,000 29,92,400 2015-16 663 2,50,000 14,52,800 3.2. Thus the assessee claimed that he is not interested in showing higher income though the basic exemption limit is not fully exhausted by the assessee. 3.3. The Ld. A.O. issued notice u/s. 133(6) to Radhe Fertilizer, however there was no response from that party. Therefore the Assessing Officer held that 50% of the agricultural income is considered to be reasonable and balance 50% namely Rs. 14,32,782/- is treated as unaccounted income brought in the guise of exempt agricultural income and thereby added to the total income of the assessee u/s. 68 r.w.s. 115BBE of the Act and also initiated penalty proceedings. 4. Aggrieved against the same, the assessee filed an appeal before Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) and made detailed submissions as follows: “…….Assessee has earned income of Rs. 13,72,140/- during the year under consideration by cultivating on his own land (42.66 v

rows.desc: EconomyRBI Forex Swap Window Attracts $136.37 Billion, FCNR(B) Deposits Drive InflowsCurated by: Vikas KumarUpdated Sep 2, 2026, 19:37 ISTFCNR(B) deposits scheme was originally open till September 30, 2026, was advanced to close on August 31, 2026, due to unexpected inflows.RBI Forex Swap Windowfollow usfollow usThe special USD-INR forex swap facility by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has attracted total inflows of $136.37 billion as of August 31, 2026, according to data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).In the total inflows, FCNR(B) deposits emerged as the dominant contributor, accounting for $127.22 billion of the total inflows. This is nearly 90 per cent of the overall figure. OFCBs added $5.26 billion, while ECBs brought in $3.89 billion.FCNR(B) deposits scheme was originally open till September 30, 2026, was advanced to close on August 31, 2026, due to unexpected inflows.A special USD-INR forex swap facility was introduced by RBI covering these instruments on June 8 this year to deal with forex outflows. This was due to high oil prices and flight of capital owing to exit of Foreign Portfolio Investors (FOIs) from the stock market. The rupee had come under pressure when these measures were announced. Readers' discretion is advised. The Nifty PSU Bank index has been hovering around its long-term 200-day moving average (200-DMA) on the technical charts for the last month. The index tested (hit) the 200-DMA in 16 out of the last 24 trading sessions, suggesting a stiff tussle between the bulls and bears at the 200-DMA, which stands at 8,601. In general, the 200-DMA is a widely used technical indicator to determine the long-term trends of the underlying index or stock. Indices or stocks trading above the 200-DMA are considered to be in an uptrend, and vice versa. Given this background, here's a detailed technical analysis on the Nifty PSU Bank and select stocks from the index by Muthuselvaraj M, Technical Research Analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan. "A breakout above the recent swing high is needed for a positive shift; otherwise, we expect consolidation between 8,200 and 8,800, with medium-term support at 8,000. Overall, the structure remains sideways to negative for the short term," says the analyst. Canara Bank Current Market Price: ₹127.76 Canara Bank stock is trading below its 200-DMA of ₹138.80, signalling that the corrective phase may continue toward the ₹126 level, with key medium-term support at ₹116, says Muthuselvaraj. Adding that, on the upside, a break above the ₹130–140 hurdle zone is required to shift the short-to-medium-term trend to positive, potentially targeting ₹148–160 levels. Bank of Baroda Current Market Price: ₹242.80 Bank of Baroda has been forming a "lower top, lower bottom" pattern since peaking at ₹325, notes the analyst. Muthuselvaraj, however, reckons that the stock appears resilient around the ₹235 level, with immediate support at ₹220. He expects the stock to consolidate between ₹235 and ₹250 in the short-term, adding that the medium-term structure looks mildly bullish. The country’s most-valuable lender’s weighting in the NSE Nifty 50 Index has shrunk to 9.81 per cent, narrowly ahead of rival ICICI Bank Ltd.’s 9.34 per cent, according to the latest data tracked by Bloomberg. The gap exceeded four percentage points at the start of the year. Reliance Industries Ltd. is currently third with a weighting of slightly above 8 per cent. HDFC Bank CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan’s surprise decision to step aside when his term ends next month has deepened uncertainty as the lender grapples with questions over its practices, first raised by its former part-time chairman. Its shares have tumbled 29 per cent so far this year, set for the worst annual performance since 2008, compared to a 4 per cent decline in the Nifty Bank Index. rows.title: RBI DG Murmu says NBFCs should use securitisation to transfer risk, free up capital
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read RBI DG Murmu says NBFCs should use securitisation to transfer risk, free up capital RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu has called for securitisation to evolve beyond a liquidity management tool into a mechanism for genuine risk transfer and capital release, while urging NBFCs and HFCs to diversify funding sources amid vulnerabilities exposed by past liquidity shocks. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 3, 2026 at 12:58 PM IST var news_msid = 133729017; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Reserve Bank of India (RBI) deputy governor Shirish Chandra MurmuThe Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu has called for securitisation to move beyond being a liquidity management tool and become a genuine mechanism for transferring risk and freeing up capital, as the non-banking financial sector enters a new phase of growth.Speaking at the 7th edition of the NBFC and HFC Summit in Mumbai, Murmu said the growing role of non bank lenders in India's credit system also brings the need for stronger foundations, particularly around liquidity management, asset quality and governance. Advt “Securitisation should also grow beyond liquidity tools into a genuine way to transfer risk and free up capital,” Murmu said, adding that this should be accompanied by appropriate scaling and transparency rules.The RBI deputy governor also flagged funding concentration as a key vulnerability for NBFCs and HFCs. Past liquidity events, he said, have demonstrated how exposed non-bank lenders can be to shifts in market sentiment and concentration in funding sources.“Strong liquidity risk management is not optional,” Murmu said, calling on entities to diversify their funding sources. He also said a deep and liquid corporate bond market would help the sector in this regard, with RBI continuing to work with market participants to develop such a market.Murmu's comments come against the backdrop of the expanding role of NBFCs in India's credit ecosystem. Credit extended by NBFCs is now above 16.7 per cent of nominal GDP, compared with 15.9 per cent a year earlier, while it accounts for about 27 per cent of the credit extended by scheduled commercial banks, up from 26 per cent a year earlier.According to Murmu, the sector is increasingly moving from being a set of alternative lenders to becoming a group of specialised financial partners that complement banks. NBFCs and HFCs have built expertise in areas including supply-chain finance, infrastructure debt, affordable housing, vehicle finance and gold and silver-backed lending. Advt This specialisation, he said, allows lenders to assess borrowers using more than traditional metrics and structure credit around their cash flows. Co-lending arrangements with banks can further extend the reach of such specialised lenders.“Growth must never come at the cost of underwriting standards,” he said.The RBI deputy governor also outlined the regulatory changes introduced over the past five to six years to strengthen the foundations of the non-banking sector. These include the comprehensive liquidity risk management framework introduced in 2019, phased capital requirements from 2020 and the scale-based regulatory framework introduced in 2021, which calibrates regulation according to an NBFC's size, activities and risk. Advt RBI subsequently consolidated the framework and introduced measures covering fraud risk management, internal audit, supervisory reporting and compliance requirements. At the same time, the central bank has taken steps intended to support sustainable growth, including regulatory flexibility for certain activities and exemptions for some smaller NBFCs from registration requirements.Murmu said RBI's approach to digital finance has also been to avoid creating a separate regulatory framework. Instead, the central bank follows the principle of “substance over form”, adapting existing rules to new digital contexts while maintaining proportionate regulation and financial stability. Advt Five priorities for NBFCsMurmu identified five priorities for sustainable growth of the sector - governance and culture, liquidity management, asset quality and credit risk, customer protection and fair conduct, and digital transformation and cyber resilience. rows.title: After record FCNR inflows, will domestic deposit rates finally fall?
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read After record FCNR inflows, will domestic deposit rates finally fall? The funding windfall could ease pressure on banks to compete aggressively for domestic deposits, particularly bulk deposits, as the FCNR(B) deposits carry regulatory advantages. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Updated On Sep 3, 2026 at 05:24 AM IST var news_msid = 133722508; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Banks mobilised $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits by August 31, taking total inflows under the swap facility to $136.38 billion.Fresh domestic term-deposit rates fell to 5.90% in July from 5.99% in June, while outstanding deposit rates remained at 6.58%.SBI cut bulk deposit rates by up to 25 basis points across several short-tenor buckets, signalling easing pressure on domestic funding costs.FCNR inflows could support bank margins by reducing reliance on expensive domestic funding, but a broad-based fall in deposit rates will depend on credit demand and deposit mobilisation.India’s record mobilisation of foreign-currency deposits is creating room for banks to reduce their dependence on expensive domestic funding, raising the prospect of further declines in deposit rates. The latest data show fresh domestic term-deposit rates have already started easing, while the scale of FCNR(B) mobilisation has significantly strengthened banks’ funding position.Banks mobilised $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank of India’s special foreign-exchange swap facility by August 31, taking total inflows under the facility to $136.38 billion, including $5.26 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings and $3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings. The FCNR(B) mobilisation window closed on August 31, while the ECB and OFCB windows remain open until December 31. Advt The funding windfall could ease pressure on banks to compete aggressively for domestic deposits, particularly bulk deposits, as the FCNR(B) deposits carry regulatory advantages. Eligible three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits mobilised under the scheme are exempt from CRR and SLR requirements, reducing the regulatory cost associated with these funds.There are already signs of moderation in domestic deposit pricing. The weighted average domestic term-deposit rate on fresh deposits declined to 5.90% in July from 5.99% in June, while the rate on outstanding deposits remained unchanged at 6.58%. The decline, however, predates the final surge in FCNR(B) mobilisation and therefore cannot be attributed solely to the foreign-currency inflows.The pressure on domestic funding costs is also visible in banks’ pricing of bulk deposits. State Bank of India cut rates on deposits of Rs 3 crore and above by 25 basis points across several short-tenor buckets from August 15, while rates on some other tenors were reduced by 10 basis points.Varied impactThe impact of the FCNR mobilisation is likely to differ across banks. Larger banks with stronger access to foreign-currency deposits may have greater scope to replace relatively expensive domestic bulk funding, whereas smaller banks could remain more dependent on domestic deposits to support credit growth. Advt The funding advantage comes at a time when the transmission of lower policy rates to bank lending rates remains uneven. Outstanding WALR on rupee loans rose marginally to 8.97% in July from 8.96% in June, while WALR on fresh loans declined marginally to 8.52% from 8.53%. The one-year median MCLR, meanwhile, increased to 8.70% in August from 8.60% in July.This divergence could become important for bank margins. If deposit costs decline faster than lending rates, banks could see some relief on their funding costs even as loan pricing remains relatively sticky. However, the benefit will not flow through immediately because a large part of banks’ existing deposit book is repriced only when deposits mature and are renewed. Advt With the FCNR(B) mobilisation window now closed, the key question is how much of the funding benefit translates into lower domestic deposit rates. The initial signs point towards easing pressure on deposit pricing, but a broad-based decline will depend on banks’ credit demand, the pace of domestic deposit mobilisation and how quickly the additional foreign-currency funding is deployed.For now, the record FCNR(B) inflow has changed the funding equation for banks, but it is too early to conclude that it will by itself trigger a sustained fall in domestic deposit rates. rows.title: Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watch
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watch Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watchIntro: While the bank has reiterated that the early retirement of managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal will not affect its FY27 guidance or near-term strategic priorities, the eventual successor will be closely watched for continuity in executing the roadmap. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 05:40 AM IST var news_msid = 133722599; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Ujjivan SFB targets a Rs 1 lakh crore loan book and 65-70% secured asset mix by FY30, with secured loans already rising to around 50%.The bank’s FY30 roadmap also targets CASA of 35%, deposits at three times Q1FY26 levels and 1,150 branches.Carol Furtado has taken interim charge as MD & CEO, while Ujjivan is expected to submit shortlisted candidates to the RBI within three to four months.Ujjivan has retained its FY27 guidance, with MSME growth and asset quality tracking broadly in line with expectations despite the leadership transition.Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s strategy to scale its gross loan book to Rs 1 lakh crore and increase the share of secured assets to 65-70% by FY30 faces a leadership transition following the early retirement of managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal on health grounds. While the bank has reiterated that the change will not affect its FY27 guidance or near-term strategic priorities, the eventual successor will be closely watched for continuity in executing the roadmap.Nautiyal, who joined Ujjivan SFB in July 2024, played a key role in accelerating the bank’s diversification, with the secured share of the loan book rising from around 31% in June 2024 to around 50% in June 2026. The bank’s FY30 roadmap also envisages CASA of 35%, a deposit base three times the Q1FY26 level, a branch network of 1,150 and a reduction in the cost-to-income ratio to 55% and credit-to-assets ratio to below 5%, according to Axis Securities. Advt The bank is targeting a further increase in secured loans to 65-70% of the portfolio by FY30 as it moves towards a more diversified asset mix. The strategy also includes building the loan book to Rs 1 lakh crore, strengthening the liability franchise and expanding its digital and physical distribution network.The leadership change comes after Nautiyal sought early retirement citing health concerns. He ceased to hold the positions of MD & CEO and key managerial personnel with effect from September 1 and will remain on leave during his three-month notice period ending November 30. The bank has maintained that his early retirement is unrelated to its strategy, governance or operations.The interim CEOCarol Furtado, the bank’s existing executive director, has been appointed interim MD & CEO for three months, with the Reserve Bank of India approving the appointment. Furtado has more than three decades of banking experience across business, strategy, operations, people and institutional functions. She had also taken charge as Officer on Special Duty and subsequently as interim CEO during an earlier leadership transition at Ujjivan in 2021.Ujjivan is expected to begin the succession process ahead of the original November timeline and submit a list of shortlisted candidates to the RBI over the next three to four months. Both internal and external candidates will be considered, with Furtado remaining a potential internal candidate for the permanent MD & CEO position. Advt Despite the leadership change, the bank has maintained its FY27 guidance and indicated that its broader diversification strategy remains on track. The MSME business is tracking in line with FY27 guidance, while asset-quality outcomes have remained better than or broadly in line with Q1 performance, with no material deviations currently visible.The bank has also appointed Vikas Agarwal as head of its MSME business as it seeks to strengthen its leadership bandwidth. Agarwal has more than 25 years of experience across MSME, business banking, retail banking, credit, product and distribution.Ujjivan has remained non-committal on the timeline for reapplying for a universal bank licence, choosing instead to focus on its broader diversification strategy. The immediate priority is therefore execution of the existing business plan, including the shift towards secured lending, strengthening the deposit franchise and expanding MSME operations. Advt The key uncertainty for investors will be whether the eventual successor maintains the strategic direction established under Nautiyal. rows.title: IBC recoveries remain stuck at just 31% of admitted claims despite Rs 4.6 lakh crore realised
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read IBC recoveries remain stuck at just 31% of admitted claims despite Rs 4.6 lakh crore realised The resolution mechanism has cumulatively resolved around Rs 14 lakh crore of debt, with creditors realising around Rs 4.6 lakh crore. While recoveries are above both fair value and liquidation benchmarks, creditors have still faced an overall haircut of around 70% to admitted claims ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 05:29 AM IST var news_msid = 133722567; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Nearly 76% of ongoing CIRPs have exceeded 270 days, while around 1,500 resolved cases took an average of 757 days.Financial creditors initiated 116 of the 177 CIRPs admitted in Q1FY27, continuing the shift away from operational-creditor-led filings.Liquidation remains significant, with 3,074 corporate debtors going into liquidation versus 1,484 resolutions, while 79% of ongoing liquidations have exceeded two years.IBC accounted for 52.4% of scheduled commercial bank recoveries in FY25, while its recovery rate improved to 37% from 28%.Creditors have realised around Rs 4.6 lakh crore through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), but recoveries remain at only around 31% of admitted claims, implying significant haircuts despite an improvement in resolution outcomes. The data highlights the continuing gap between the value of claims admitted and the amount ultimately recovered by creditors.The IBC has cumulatively resolved around Rs 14 lakh crore of debt, with creditors realising around Rs 4.6 lakh crore. While recoveries are above both fair value and liquidation benchmarks, creditors have still faced an overall haircut of around 70% to admitted claims, according to Kotak Institutional Equities. Advt Deep haircuts are particularly evident in large resolved cases. Jaiprakash Associates, which was resolved in the fourth quarter of FY26, had admitted claims of around Rs 60,600 crore, with creditors recovering around 23% of claims, equivalent to about 89% of the liquidation value.Timelines stretchResolution timelines continue to weigh on the effectiveness of the insolvency framework. Nearly 76% of ongoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes (CIRPs) had exceeded the 270-day threshold as of June 2026. Around 1,500 resolved cases have taken an average of 757 days, indicating that the IBC's objective of time-bound resolution remains unmet.During the first quarter of FY27, 177 CIRPs were admitted, broadly implying a run-rate consistent with FY26, when 668 cases were admitted. Financial creditors initiated 116 of the 177 cases during the quarter, continuing the shift away from operational-creditor-led filings.Of the 156 CIRPs closed during the quarter, 69 resulted in approved resolution plans. The resolution-to-liquidation ratio has improved steadily to an all-time high of 1.28, suggesting a recent shift towards resolution-led outcomes.However, liquidation remains a common outcome for companies entering the insolvency resolution process. Cumulatively, 3,074 corporate debtors have gone into liquidation compared with 1,484 resolutions, with liquidation accounting for 42% of closures. As of June 2026, 79% of ongoing liquidations had exceeded two years. Advt The recovery performance of the IBC has nevertheless improved for banks. The IBC contributed Rs 54,000 crore of the Rs 1.04 lakh crore total scheduled commercial bank recoveries in FY2025, accounting for 52.4% of recoveries. The IBC recovery rate improved to 37% from 28%.Operational-creditor-led cases tend to conclude through early settlements, while financial-creditor-led cases are more likely to proceed through resolution or liquidation. Manufacturing remains the largest contributor, accounting for around 40% of admitted resolution plans.Recent reforms aimed at faster admission through information utility records and greater flexibility in structuring resolutions are expected to improve timelines and recovery outcomes at the margin. At the same time, the broader IBC data points to a relatively benign corporate credit cycle, with strong corporate balance sheets, modest leverage and a capex cycle broadly funded through operating cash flows limiting near-term asset-quality risks for lenders. rows.title: India stalls Alipay+ payments link over security, data concerns, sources say
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read India stalls Alipay+ payments link over security, data concerns, sources say India has stalled Alipay+'s proposal to link with its instant payments system. National security concerns and data usage questions are the primary reasons for this decision. The Indian government cited political grounds for halting the integration of the payment platforms. Law enforcement agencies also raised concerns about money laundering and data breaches. Sumedha Tripathi Reuters Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 02:58 PM IST var news_msid = 133731768; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Alipay+'s proposal to link with India's instant payments system for cross-border transactions has ​been stalled due to national security concerns in ​New Delhi and questions about the storage and use of customer data, three sources familiar with ​the discussions said.The proposal, made by Alipay+ in January, was the first by a China-linked entity in the financial services sector and came against the backdrop of easing tensions between the two neighbours, which had a deadly border clash in 2020.New Delhi and Beijing are working on maintaining peace ‌at the border and ⁠Chinese ⁠President Xi Jinping's expected visit to attend a BRICS summit in New Delhi later this month has been viewed as an effort to stabilise bilateral relations. Advt The Indian ​government's concerns about Alipay+'s proposal stem from its Chinese links, data-security risks and the potential misuse of customer data, the three sources said. ​The sources requested anonymity because the discussions are confidential. Reuters is reporting for the first time the Indian government's views on the matter.Alipay+ is operated by Singapore-based Ant International, a digital payments and fintech firm that was spun out of China's Ant Group as an independent company in 2024.India's ministries of external affairs, finance, home affairs, the ⁠Reserve Bank ‌of India, the National Payments Corporation of India and Ant International did not respond to requests ​for comment.'POLITICAL GROUNDS' Alipay+ proposed ​linking with India's instant payments system, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), to allow Indian travellers in China, ⁠Hong Kong and other parts of Asia to make payments at more than ​150 million merchants in its network, Reuters reported at the time. The second phase of ​the proposal would have allowed international visitors to use Alipay+ in India.India's foreign ministry cited "political grounds" as the reason to stall the proposal, one of the three sources said, adding that there was no clear path to clearing the hurdles that stand in its way. Advt Indian law enforcement agencies have raised concerns about potential money-laundering risks and the threat of data breaches that could expose customers to cyberfraud, according to two of the sources.A third source said how transaction data is processed, stored and managed, and ‌processes for dispute resolution are part of the checks made for all bilateral cross-border payment programmes, but the scrutiny is significantly higher for China-linked entities.India's financial services sector remains closely guarded, one of the ​sources said, even after ​the country eased some restrictions on ⁠Chinese companies in March. Advt The restrictions on Chinese investments were put in place after the 2020 border clash.LINKING REGIONAL PAYMENT SYSTEMSThe proposal to link Alipay+ with UPI comes as the two payment systems seek to broaden their regional partnerships in countries like Malaysia, ​the Philippines, South Korea, Singapore and France.Countries in Asia, in an effort to cut costs and enable faster cross-border payments, have lately been linking their existing payment systems.The market size for outbound cross-border payments from the Asia-Pacific region is expected to reach $23.8 trillion by 2032, nearly doubling from 2024, according to data provider FXC Intelligence. Advt The third source said national security concerns have clouded the decision-making process, despite the benefits that a link between Alipay+ and UPI could bring to cross-border payments. rows.title: Aditya Birla Group gets Rs 24,000 crore bank commitments for Shell deal, 70% more than planned
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Aditya Birla Group gets Rs 24,000 crore bank commitments for Shell deal, 70% more than planned Aditya Birla Group secured loan commitments exceeding its initial acquisition funding needs. Axis Bank and State Bank of India offered substantial credit lines to the conglomerate. Union Bank and Punjab National Bank also provided significant credit facilities for the deal. This acquisition will transfer control of Shell's Indian renewable energy portfolio. Indian lenders show strong appetite for large corporate deals in the market. Saikat Das Bloomberg Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 02:08 PM IST var news_msid = 133730735; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook A unit of billionaire Kumar Mangalam Birla’s conglomerate has received as much as 240 billion rupees ($2.5 billion) in commitments from at least four banks for an acquisition loan, 70% more than what it was planning for, according to people familiar with the matter.Aditya Birla Group is seeking a 140 billion-rupee loan to finance the acquisition of Shell Plc’s renewable energy assets in India. Axis Bank and State Bank of India have each committed up to 70 billion rupees, while Union Bank of India and Punjab National Bank have offered credit lines of around 50 billion rupees apiece, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. The actual disbursements would be less than those ceilings, they said. Advt Also read: Aditya Birla Group taps local lenders for Sprng EnergyThe conglomerate is also in discussions with a few other large banks including HDFC Bank Ltd. and Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd., which could also extend credit lines, the people said.Representatives for Aditya Birla Group, Axis Bank, State Bank of India, Union Bank of India, Punjab National Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.The commitments underscore the strong appetite from Indian lenders for large corporate deals as they compete with global peers in financing big acquisitions in the country’s $40 billion-plus deals market. The Reserve Bank of India began allowing local banks to finance corporate acquisitions from July 1 in a bid to spur the economy.Aditya Birla Renewables Ltd. will acquire 100% of Solenergi Power Pvt. to take control of its 5-gigawatt portfolio in the country. Solenergi owns Sprng Energy, which operates Shell’s renewables assets in India.Also read: Aditya Birla Group levies royalty on Grasim, Hindalco, Novelis for brand use from June 2026Interest rates on the club loan ranged from 7.6% to 7.7% with tenors of 12 to 20 years, the people said, adding it’s being taken by multiple special purpose vehicles backed by the company.Loans extended by Indian banks grew 18.3% to 220 trillion rupees between January to Aug. 15, outpacing the 14.7% increase in deposits, central bank data show. India’s banking sector is likely to see a flood of liquidity after the country raised a record $127 billion from its vast diaspora through an aggressive push by lenders which is expected to drive down borrowing costs.
